steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on self-contradictory hallucinations in large language models, covering how we evaluate, detect, and mitigate them for black-box LMs. Organize it with short subsections for the main idea, why it matters, the results, generality, and the released tool and code.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - large LMs pretrained on massive corpora, fine-tuned to follow instructions
  - instruction-tuned LMs (ChatGPT): remarkable zero-shot capabilities
  - increasingly integrated into daily life: online search, professional environments
  - even ChatGPT and GPT-4 generate nonsensical/unfaithful content = hallucinations
  - concerns about trustworthiness
  - detecting/mitigating hallucinations still open, esp. for proprietary black-box LMs

## Reasoning about Self-contradictory Hallucinations
- self-contradiction: two logically inconsistent sentences, same context
- key insight: use self-contradiction to tackle non-factual outputs
  - guaranteed to reveal non-factuality: two contradicting sentences can't both be correct
  - removing conflicting info strictly decreases non-factuality
  - detection and removal via logical reasoning, a strength of modern LMs
  - no need for externally retrieved knowledge or comparing tens of samples (difficult/expensive)
- three-step pipeline
  - trigger: constraints to generate relevant sentence pairs
  - detect: existing prompting strategies
  - mitigate: iterative local text edits, keep fluency and informativeness
  - prompting only -> works on black-box LMs

## Significance of Self-contradiction
- evaluation on four modern LMs: GPT-4, ChatGPT, Llama2-70B-Chat, Vicuna-13B
- main focus: open-domain text generation (long text from LMs' internal knowledge); trustworthiness desired but hard
- self-contradictions prevalent: e.g. 17.7% of all ChatGPT sentences in open-domain generation
- large portion (e.g. 35.2% for ChatGPT) not verifiable with Wikipedia or web search text
- -> complement to retrieval-based approaches

## Effective Detection and Mitigation
- detection e.g. \sim 80% F1 score
- mitigation: up to 89.5% of self-contradictions removed, informativeness and fluency kept
- Table 1: two ChatGPT self-contradictions triggered, detected, mitigated
- Appendix C: longer examples, sentence and text level

## Generality
- applied to question answering
- precision e.g. 74.2% to 83.8%; detects e.g. 12.7% to 38.0% self-contradictions
- vanilla and retrieval-augmented QA

## User-friendly Tool and Open-source Repository
- effectiveness + generality -> practicality
- tool: warnings for hallucinations + automatic mitigation, https://chatprotect.ai/
- code and datasets on GitHub: https://github.com/eth-sri/ChatProtect

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (large LMs) are pretrained on massive text corpora and then fine-tuned to follow human instructions. Instruction-tuned LMs like ChatGPT have shown remarkable zero-shot capabilities at solving natural language tasks. Because of this, they are being integrated more and more into various parts of daily life, including online search and professional environments. But even widely adopted LMs like ChatGPT and GPT-4 tend to generate nonsensical or unfaithful content, which is commonly called hallucinations. This raises big concerns about whether LMs can be trusted. Detecting and mitigating hallucinations is still an open challenge, especially for state-of-the-art proprietary LMs that are only accessible as black boxes.

## Reasoning about Self-contradictory Hallucinations

This work focuses on an important type of hallucination called self-contradiction. Self-contradiction happens when an LM generates two sentences that are logically inconsistent given the same context. Our key insight is that self-contradiction can be used to conveniently tackle non-factual model outputs. We use the fact that self-contradiction is guaranteed to reveal non-factuality, since two contradicting sentences cannot both be correct at the same time. Also, removing the conflicting information from a pair of contradictory sentences strictly decreases non-factuality. Importantly, both detecting and removing contradictions can be done by logical reasoning, which is a particular strength of modern LMs. This means we do not have to rely on externally retrieved knowledge or compare tens of samples, which can be difficult or too expensive in practice.

Based on this insight, we propose a pipeline with three steps for reasoning about self-contradictions. First, to trigger self-contradictions, we use appropriate constraints to generate relevant pairs of sentences. Then, we explore various existing prompting strategies to detect self-contradictions. Lastly, we develop an iterative mitigation procedure that makes local edits to the text to remove contradictory information, while keeping other important qualities of the text such as fluency and informativeness. Our framework works through prompting, so it can be applied directly to state-of-the-art black-box LMs.

## Significance of Self-contradiction
- evaluation on four modern LMs: GPT-4, ChatGPT, Llama2-70B-Chat, Vicuna-13B
- main focus: open-domain text generation (long text from LMs' internal knowledge); trustworthiness desired but hard
- self-contradictions prevalent: e.g. 17.7% of all ChatGPT sentences in open-domain generation
- large portion (e.g. 35.2% for ChatGPT) not verifiable with Wikipedia or web search text
- -> complement to retrieval-based approaches

## Effective Detection and Mitigation
- detection e.g. \sim 80% F1 score
- mitigation: up to 89.5% of self-contradictions removed, informativeness and fluency kept
- Table 1: two ChatGPT self-contradictions triggered, detected, mitigated
- Appendix C: longer examples, sentence and text level

## Generality
- applied to question answering
- precision e.g. 74.2% to 83.8%; detects e.g. 12.7% to 38.0% self-contradictions
- vanilla and retrieval-augmented QA

## User-friendly Tool and Open-source Repository
- effectiveness + generality -> practicality
- tool: warnings for hallucinations + automatic mitigation, https://chatprotect.ai/
- code and datasets on GitHub: https://github.com/eth-sri/ChatProtect

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (large LMs) are pretrained on massive text corpora and then fine-tuned to follow human instructions. Instruction-tuned LMs like ChatGPT have shown remarkable zero-shot capabilities at solving natural language tasks. Because of this, they are being integrated more and more into various parts of daily life, including online search and professional environments. But even widely adopted LMs like ChatGPT and GPT-4 tend to generate nonsensical or unfaithful content, which is commonly called hallucinations. This raises big concerns about whether LMs can be trusted. Detecting and mitigating hallucinations is still an open challenge, especially for state-of-the-art proprietary LMs that are only accessible as black boxes.

## Reasoning about Self-contradictory Hallucinations

This work focuses on an important type of hallucination called self-contradiction. Self-contradiction happens when an LM generates two sentences that are logically inconsistent given the same context. Our key insight is that self-contradiction can be used to conveniently tackle non-factual model outputs. We use the fact that self-contradiction is guaranteed to reveal non-factuality, since two contradicting sentences cannot both be correct at the same time. Also, removing the conflicting information from a pair of contradictory sentences strictly decreases non-factuality. Importantly, both detecting and removing contradictions can be done by logical reasoning, which is a particular strength of modern LMs. This means we do not have to rely on externally retrieved knowledge or compare tens of samples, which can be difficult or too expensive in practice.

Based on this insight, we propose a pipeline with three steps for reasoning about self-contradictions. First, to trigger self-contradictions, we use appropriate constraints to generate relevant pairs of sentences. Then, we explore various existing prompting strategies to detect self-contradictions. Lastly, we develop an iterative mitigation procedure that makes local edits to the text to remove contradictory information, while keeping other important qualities of the text such as fluency and informativeness. Our framework works through prompting, so it can be applied directly to state-of-the-art black-box LMs.

## Significance of Self-contradiction

We do an extensive evaluation on four modern LMs: GPT-4, ChatGPT, Llama2-70B-Chat, and Vicuna-13B. We mainly focus on open-domain text generation, which is a task where LMs produce long text using their internal knowledge, and where trustworthiness is very much wanted but hard to achieve. Our evaluation shows that self-contradiction is significant. Specifically, self-contradictions are common across the LMs we evaluated, for example in 17.7% of all sentences generated by ChatGPT in open-domain text generation. A large part of these (for example 35.2% for ChatGPT) cannot be verified using Wikipedia or text obtained by web search. This means our work is a valuable complement to retrieval-based approaches.

## Effective Detection and Mitigation

Our framework is highly effective at detecting self-contradictions (e.g., \sim 80% F1 score) and at mitigating them (e.g., reducing up to 89.5% of self-contradictions while keeping text informativeness and fluency). Table 1 shows two instances of self-contradictions generated by ChatGPT that our method successfully triggers, detects, and mitigates. Appendix C gives various longer examples, at both the sentence and the text level.

## Generality

We also apply our method to question answering. The results show that our approach detects a significant number (e.g., 12.7% to 38.0%) of self-contradictions, and does so accurately (e.g., 74.2% to 83.8% precision), for both vanilla and retrieval-augmented question answering.

## User-friendly Tool and Open-source Repository

Our framework is effective and general, which shows that it is practical. We release a user-friendly tool that gives warnings for hallucinations and automatically mitigates them, available at https://chatprotect.ai/. Our code and datasets are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/eth-sri/ChatProtect.

## Reasoning about Self-contradictory Hallucinations

This work focuses on an important type of hallucination called self-contradiction. Self-contradiction happens when an LM generates two sentences that are logically inconsistent given the same context. Based on this insight, we propose a three-step pipeline for reasoning about self-contradictions. To trigger self-contradictions, we employ appropriate constraints to generate relevant sentence pairs. Then, we explore various existing prompting strategies to detect self-contradictions [24,25,26]. Lastly, we develop an iterative mitigation procedure that makes local text edits to remove contradictory information while preserving other important text qualities, such as fluency and informativeness. Since our framework operates through prompting, it is directly applicable to state-of-the-art black-box LMs.

## Significance of Self-contradiction

We perform an extensive evaluation on four modern LMs: GPT-4 [9], ChatGPT [5], Llama2-70B-Chat [27], and Vicuna-13B [28]. We primarily focus on open-domain text generation, a task that involves producing long text using LMs' internal knowledge [29,30], where trustworthiness is highly desired but challenging to achieve [18]. Our evaluation highlights the significance of self-contradiction: self-contradictions are prevalent across the evaluated LMs, e.g., in 17.7% of all sentences generated by ChatGPT in open-domain text generation. A large portion of these (e.g., 35.2% for ChatGPT) cannot be verified using Wikipedia or text obtained by web search. In other words, our work is a valuable complement to retrieval-based approaches [31,22,32].

## Effective Detection and Mitigation

Our proposed framework is highly effective at detecting (e.g., \sim 80% F1 score) and mitigating self-contradictions (e.g., reducing up to 89.5% of self-contradictions while maintaining text informativeness and fluency). In Table 1, we present two instances of ChatGPT-generated self-contradictions that are successfully triggered, detected, and mitigated by our method. Appendix C provides various longer examples, at both the sentence and text levels.

## Generality

We further apply our method to question answering [33]. The results show that our approach accurately (e.g., 74.2% to 83.8% precision) detects a significant number (e.g., 12.7% to 38.0%) of self-contradictions, for both vanilla and retrieval-augmented question answering.

## User-friendly Tool and Open-source Repository

The effectiveness and generality of our framework demonstrate its practicality. We release a user-friendly tool that produces warnings for hallucinations and automatically mitigates them, accessible at https://chatprotect.ai/. Our code and datasets are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/eth-sri/ChatProtect.
